title: Boulevard gardens rules and natural heritage protection
subtitle: Urban forest strategy update, office furniture contract, older adult program agreement, and a reaffirmed commitment to green space.
overview: Council updated the rules for boulevard and cul-de-sac gardens by amending three by-laws, and directed staff to report back on artificial turf {{vote:m4}}. Existing gardens will be grandfathered in. Staff proposed shrinking the buffer strip between naturalized areas and lawns, and the by-law amendments were enacted later in the meeting {{vote:m8}}.

Council also received the first Urban Forest Management Strategy report as information {{vote:m3}}, with public consultation planned for 2024. It approved a contract with Teknion Limited for office furniture {{vote:m5}} and the signing of a provincial accountability agreement for older adult programs {{vote:m6}}. The mayor's motion reaffirming the city's practice of acquiring and protecting natural heritage areas and green space was also approved {{vote:m7}}.

For residents, the changes mean clearer gardening rules on boulevards, more room for naturalized lawns, and an early look at how the city may protect and grow its tree canopy. Council met in closed session earlier in the afternoon on committee appointments, a potential land lease and an OLT appeal; the minutes report no public outcome. Councillors also thanked staff and volunteers for recent community events.

decisions.detail: Council approved the report and amended the Highway Occupancy, Lot Maintenance and Administrative Penalties by-laws, and received the garden guideline as information.
Council directed staff to report back on the use of artificial turf.
Council reaffirmed its longstanding practice of acquiring and protecting sensitive natural heritage areas and green spaces and managing growth sustainably.
Council awarded RFQ23-27 to Teknion Limited for a total of $649,459.72 including unrecoverable HST.
Council authorized the Mayor to sign the Multi-Sector Service Accountability Agreement declaration of compliance and related documents.
Council received the strategy report as information, with public consultation to follow.

debate: On the urban forest strategy, councillors asked whether a private tree by-law could work. Staff said some Ontario municipalities have one and that it needs balanced implementation. One councillor worried it could fuel neighbour disputes.
Staff said the immediate challenge is keeping the existing canopy as intensification continues. About 900 trees are planted each year, close to what current staffing allows.
A resident delegate said monthly grass-length notices felt like a poor use of resources. The delegate asked for a higher grass limit and no buffer strip around naturalized areas.

Staff said the buffer strip would drop from one metre to 30 cm. They explained that officers cannot reliably identify invasive species, and the by-law covers noxious weeds only through a general clause. Some councillors asked for a clearer definition of undesirable material, and staff agreed to improve public information.

Councillors discussed buffer strips and artificial turf. Buffer strips keep sidewalks and roads clear, but one councillor warned of overgrown sidewalks. On turf, concerns included effects on insects and permeability, while another councillor noted accessibility reasons for using it. Staff said planning is already reviewing turf.
